claims.evidence: This is a statement of the study's findings.

claims.claim: Dopamine neurons projecting to TS are a clear outlier in terms of their inputs.
claims.source: We found that populations of dopamine neurons projecting to most of these targets receive a similar set of inputs, while dopamine neurons projecting to TS ('tail of the striatum' or 'posterior striatum') are a clear outlier.
claims.evidence: This is a statement of the study's findings.

claims.claim: Classifying dopamine neurons based on their projection target is a viable approach.
claims.source: These results indicate that classifying dopamine neurons based on their projection target is a viable approach, and lay a foundation for studying the mechanisms by which dopamine neurons are regulated.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the study's findings.

claims.claim: The authors used a retrograde transsynaptic tracing system based on a modified rabies virus (SADΔG-EGFP(EnvA)) to visualize the monosynaptic inputs to dopamine neurons.
claims.source: To visualize the monosynaptic inputs to dopamine neurons, we used a retrograde transsynaptic tracing system based on a modified rabies virus (SADΔG-EGFP(EnvA)) (Wickersham et al., 2007).
claims.evidence: This is a statement of the study's methodology with a citation to the technique.

claims.claim: The rabies virus used is pseudotyped with an avian sarcoma and leukemia virus (ALSV-A) envelope protein (EnvA), so that the initial infection is restricted to cells that express a cognate receptor (TVA) in mammalian brains.
claims.source: This rabies virus is pseudotyped with an avian sarcoma and leukemia virus (ALSV-A) envelope protein (EnvA), so that the initial infection is restricted to cells that express a cognate receptor (TVA) in mammalian brains.
claims.evidence: This is a description of the technical properties of the rabies virus used.

claims.claim: The rabies virus used lacks the gene encoding the rabies virus envelope glycoprotein (RG), which is required for trans-synaptic spread.
claims.source: In addition, this rabies virus lacks the gene encoding the rabies virus envelope glycoprotein (RG), which is required for trans-synaptic spread.
claims.evidence: This is a description of the technical properties of the rabies virus used.

claims.claim: Only monosynaptic (but not poly-synaptic) inputs are trans-synaptically labeled using this rabies virus system.
claims.source: This allows us to restrict trans-synaptic spread to cells that exogenously express RG. In this way, only monosynaptic (but not poly-synaptic) inputs are trans-synaptically labeled.
claims.evidence: This is a description of the technical properties of the rabies virus system.

claims.claim: The authors injected helper viruses (AAV5-FLEX-TVA-mCherry and AAV8-FLEX-RG) into the VTA or SNc of transgenic mice expressing Cre specifically in dopamine neurons (dopamine transporter-Cre, or DAT-Cre) to specifically label the monosynaptic inputs of these dopamine neurons throughout the brain.
claims.source: In our previous work, we used two helper viruses to express TVA and RG under the control of Cre recombinase (AAV5-FLEX-TVA-mCherry and AAV8-FLEX-RG) (Watabe-Uchida et al., 2012). We previously injected these helper viruses into the VTA or SNc of transgenic mice expressing Cre specifically in dopamine neurons (dopamine transporter-Cre, or DAT-Cre) (Backman et al., 2006) to specifically label the monosynaptic inputs of these dopamine neurons throughout the brain (Watabe-Uchida et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: This is a description of prior methodology with citations.

claims.claim: The authors injected a helper virus that expresses TVA under the control of Cre recombinase (AAV5-FLEX-TVA) into a dopamine projection site to restrict the initial rabies infection to subpopulations of dopamine neurons defined by their projection sites.
claims.source: In the present study, we sought to restrict the initial rabies infection to subpopulations of dopamine neurons defined by their projection sites. To do this, we injected a helper virus that expresses TVA under the control of Cre recombinase (AAV5-FLEX-TVA) into a dopamine projection site and co-injected a virus bearing blue fluorescent protein (AAV1-CA-BFP) to mark this site.
claims.evidence: This is a statement of the study's methodology.

claims.claim: Minute TVA expression is sufficient for infection by ALSV-A.
claims.source: Because it has been shown that minute TVA expression is sufficient for infection by ALSV-A (Belanger et al., 1995), we reasoned that DAT-Cre-expressing dopamine neurons in the midbrain which were retrogradely infected by AAV5-FLEX-TVA would express enough TVA for initial rabies infection in a Cre-dependent manner (Figure 1A).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior work.

claims.claim: Almost all of the GFP-positive neurons (98 ± 1%; n = 600 neurons, n = 3 mice) were also positive for TH after rabies infection.
claims.source: Based on antibody staining, almost all of the GFP-positive neurons were also positive for TH (Figure 1C–F), a marker for dopamine neurons (98 ± 1%; n = 600 neurons, n = 3 mice).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by data from antibody staining shown in Figure 1C-F.

claims.claim: Injecting pseudotyped rabies virus alone resulted in very few infections.
claims.source: Given that injecting pseudotyped rabies virus alone resulted in very few infections (Watabe-Uchida et al., 2012), these results indicate that the injection of AAV5-FLEX-TVA into a dopamine projection site allowed us to restrict infection of rabies virus to dopamine neurons in a projection specific manner.
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior work.

claims.claim: The injection of AAV5-FLEX-TVA into a dopamine projection site allowed the authors to restrict infection of rabies virus to dopamine neurons in a projection specific manner.
claims.source: Given that injecting pseudotyped rabies virus alone resulted in very few infections (Watabe-Uchida et al., 2012), these results indicate that the injection of AAV5-FLEX-TVA into a dopamine projection site allowed us to restrict infection of rabies virus to dopamine neurons in a projection specific manner.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental results.

claims.claim: 77 of 89 processed brains (∼87%) were sufficiently clear for visualization of the ventral-most cells after CLARITY processing.
claims.source: 77 of 89 processed brains (∼87%) were sufficiently clear for visualization of the ventral-most cells, and only these brains were used.
claims.evidence: This is a statement of the data quality control results.

claims.claim: The authors imaged each brain from the dorsal and ventral sides and then merged these images to create a continuous 3D image of the brain.
claims.source: We imaged each brain from the dorsal and ventral sides (such that each image was a 'horizontal' optical section), and then merged these images to create a continuous 3D image of the brain (Figure 2B).
claims.evidence: This is a statement of the imaging methodology, with reference to Figure 2B.

claims.claim: The authors applied multiple segmentation algorithms to classify each pixel as 'cell' or 'non-cell'.
claims.source: We applied multiple segmentation algorithms to this data to classify each pixel as 'cell' or 'non-cell' (Figure 2D; see 'Materials and methods').
claims.evidence: This is a statement of the analysis methodology, with reference to Figure 2D.

claims.claim: The authors collapsed all neighboring 'cell' pixels in all three dimensions to generate a list of the centroids of the detected cells.
claims.source: Because each cell was present in several images (at different depths), we then collapsed all neighboring 'cell' pixels in all three dimensions to generate a list of the centroids of the detected cells.
claims.evidence: This is a statement of the analysis methodology.

claims.claim: The authors aligned the autofluorescence image captured from each brain to a common 'reference space' and used these transformations to align each set of centroids into this common space.
claims.source: To compare the distribution of cells across brains, we aligned the autofluorescence image captured from each brain to a common 'reference space' and used these transformations to align each set of centroids into this common space (see 'Materials and methods').
claims.evidence: This is a statement of the analysis methodology.

claims.claim: Dopamine neurons with distinct projection targets reside in different, but overlapping, areas of the midbrain.
claims.source: As previously reported, we found that dopamine neurons with distinct projection targets reside in different, but overlapping, areas of the midbrain (Figure 3; Figure 3—figure supplement 1; Figure 3—figure supplement 2; Figure 3—figure supplement 3) (Swanson, 1982; Bjorklund and Dunnett, 2007; Lammel et al., 2008; Haber, 2014).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by data shown in figures and citations to prior work.

claims.claim: The authors observed an overlapping but dorso-laterally shifted distribution of dopamine neurons that project to VS, DS, and TS, in this order.
claims.source: Interestingly, we observed an overlapping but dorso-laterally shifted distribution of dopamine neurons that project to VS, DS, and TS, in this order (Figure 3—figure supplement 1; Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by data shown in figures.

claims.claim: Amy-projecting dopamine neurons were labeled throughout VTA/SNc and also substantially in supramammillary areas (A10rv).
claims.source: In the case of Amy-projecting dopamine neurons, we observed labeling throughout VTA/SNc and also substantial labeling in supramammillary areas (A10rv) (Yetnikoff et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by data from the study and a citation.

claims.claim: The distribution of labeled neurons in the VTA/SNc was similar in cases with and without transsynaptic spread (with and without RG, respectively).
claims.source: Furthermore, we found that the distribution of labeled neurons in the VTA/SNc was similar in cases with and without transsynaptic spread (with and without RG, respectively), indicating that transsynaptic spread between primarily infected dopamine neurons and other dopamine neurons did not lead to the nonspecific infection of all dopamine neurons (Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claims.claim: The overall distribution of inputs to TS-projecting dopamine neurons is different from those of the rest of the dopamine neuron populations.
claims.source: However, we found that TS-projecting dopamine neurons did not show a similar concentration of inputs: these neurons received many fewer inputs from anterior regions (Figure 3A,B) and ventromedial regions (Figure 3C,D). In short, these observations suggested that the overall distribution of inputs to TS-projecting dopamine neurons is different from those of the rest of the dopamine neuron populations (whose inputs largely overlapped with one another).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by data shown in Figure 3.

claims.claim: The basal ganglia and hypothalamus provided the majority of inputs to dopamine neurons.
claims.source: Although we found some differences between subpopulations, the overall patterns were surprisingly similar. Among the brain systems, we found that the basal ganglia and hypothalamus provided the majority of inputs to dopamine neurons (Figure 4, Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by data shown in Figure 4.

claims.claim: In the basal ganglia, the ventral striatum (nucleus accumbens core and shell), DS and ventral pallidum were the largest sources of inputs.
claims.source: In the basal ganglia, the ventral striatum (nucleus accumbens core and shell), DS and ventral pallidum were the largest sources of inputs.
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by data from the study.

claims.claim: In hypothalamus, the lateral hypothalamus (LH) (including the parasubthalamic nucleus [PSTh]) contained the largest number of inputs.
claims.source: In hypothalamus, the lateral hypothalamus (LH) (including the parasubthalamic nucleus [PSTh]) contained the largest number of inputs, and the preoptic areas also provided a substantial number.
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by data from the study.

claims.claim: In the midbrain, the superior colliculus and dorsal raphe provided inputs to dopamine neurons.
claims.source: In the midbrain, the superior colliculus and dorsal raphe provided inputs as well.
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by data from the study.

claims.claim: The ventral striatum is one of the largest sources of inputs to most of the subpopulations, but is a relatively minor source of inputs to TS-projecting dopamine neurons.
claims.source: In spite of similarities among dopamine populations, several prominent differences emerge upon focusing on TS-projecting dopamine neurons. While the ventral striatum is one of the largest sources of inputs to most of the subpopulations, it is a relatively minor source of inputs to TS-projecting dopamine neurons (Figure 3A, Figure 4).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by data shown in Figure 3A and Figure 4.

claims.claim: TS-projecting neurons receive an increased proportion of their inputs from the GP, entopeduncular nucleus (EP), PSTh, subthalamic nucleus (STh) and zona incerta (ZI).
claims.source: Instead, TS-projecting neurons receive an increased proportion of their inputs from the GP (Figure 3C, Figure 4), entopeduncular nucleus (EP, Figure 3D, Figure 4), PSTh, subthalamic nucleus (STh) and zona incerta (ZI) (Figure 3E, Figure 4).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by data shown in Figure 3 and Figure 4.

claims.claim: After correcting for multiple comparisons, nucleus accumbens shell, GP, STh and ZI remained significant (p = 0.00045, 0.0017, 0.00023, and 0.0028, respectively) in 1-way ANOVA among the 20 main input areas.
claims.source: To statistically verify these observations, we first performed a 1-way analysis of variance (ANOVA) among the 20 main input areas (Figure 4—figure supplement 1). After correcting for multiple comparisons, nucleus accumbens shell, GP, STh and ZI remained significant (p = 0.00045, 0.0017, 0.00023, and 0.0028, respectively; significant after Holm-Sidak corrections for multiple comparisons).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by statistical analysis of the data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: These differences in inputs are mainly attributable to the effect of the TS-projecting dopamine population.
claims.source: These differences are mainly attributable to the effect of the TS-projecting dopamine population.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the statistical analysis.

claims.claim: If TS is removed from the analysis, none of the areas retain statistical significance with the exception of the ventromedial hypothalamus (p = 0.0028, 1-way ANOVA).
claims.source: If we remove TS in the analysis, none of these areas retain statistical significance with the exception of the ventromedial hypothalamus (p = 0.0028, 1-way ANOVA), which appears to be a slightly larger source of inputs to VS-projecting dopamine neurons.
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by statistical analysis of the data.

claims.claim: In all cases where percentage of inputs differed significantly, the percentage of inputs from TS was significantly larger than the group mean of the remainder of the populations (p < 0.001; t-test).
claims.source: Furthermore, in all of the above cases, the percentage of inputs from TS was significantly larger than the group mean of the remainder of the populations (p < 0.001; t-test).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by statistical analysis of the data.

claims.claim: Many dopamine neurons are embedded in a 'canonical' circuit similar to VS-projecting dopamine neurons, while TS-projecting dopamine neurons have a unique distribution of inputs and therefore form a distinct class of dopamine neurons.
claims.source: These results suggest that many dopamine neurons are embedded in a 'canonical' circuit similar to VS-projecting dopamine neurons (which are known to encode RPE), while TS-projecting dopamine neurons have a unique distribution of inputs and therefore form a distinct class of dopamine neurons.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the data analysis.

claims.claim: DS-projecting dopamine neurons received more inputs from the neocortex than other populations.
claims.source: For example, DS-projecting dopamine neurons received more inputs from the neocortex than other populations (Figure 4), while VS-projecting dopamine neurons received more inputs from the olfactory tubercle and other ventromedial structures such as the ventromedial hypothalamus (Figure 4).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by data shown in Figure 4.

claims.claim: VS-projecting dopamine neurons received more inputs from the olfactory tubercle and other ventromedial structures such as the ventromedial hypothalamus.
claims.source: For example, DS-projecting dopamine neurons received more inputs from the neocortex than other populations (Figure 4), while VS-projecting dopamine neurons received more inputs from the olfactory tubercle and other ventromedial structures such as the ventromedial hypothalamus (Figure 4).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by data shown in Figure 4.

claims.claim: DS-projecting and OFC-projecting dopamine neurons appeared to receive more inputs from the dorsal-most part of the DS.
claims.source: Furthermore, DS-projecting and OFC-projecting dopamine neurons appeared to receive more inputs from the dorsal-most part of the DS (Figure 3B).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by data shown in Figure 3B.

claims.claim: All populations received inputs from the dorsal raphe, but lHb-projecting dopamine neurons received fewer inputs from nearby areas.
claims.source: In the posterior midbrain, all populations received inputs from the dorsal raphe, but lHb-projecting dopamine neurons received fewer inputs from nearby areas (Figure 3H).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by data shown in Figure 3H.

claims.claim: lHb-projecting dopamine neurons received fewer inputs from posterior midbrain regions such as the periaqueductal grey and gigantocellular reticular nuclei.
claims.source: In addition, lHb-projecting dopamine neurons received fewer inputs from posterior midbrain regions such as the periaqueductal grey and gigantocellular reticular nuclei (Figure 4).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by data shown in Figure 4.

claims.claim: Most pairs of dopamine populations had relatively high correlations (r = 0.85–0.98) in their input patterns.
claims.source: We found that most pairs had relatively high correlations (r = 0.85–0.98).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by correlation analysis of the data.

claims.claim: TS-projecting dopamine neurons had consistently lower correlations than other populations in pair-wise comparisons.
claims.source: Here again, TS-projecting dopamine neurons had consistently lower correlations than other populations (Figure 5A): TS-projecting dopamine neurons were most distinct from VS- and DS-projecting dopamine neurons (r = 0.65 and 0.69, respectively) (Figure 5A), although the similarity was slightly higher compared to non-striatal regions (r = 0.69–0.82).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 5A.

claims.claim: Hierarchical clustering supported the view that TS-projecting dopamine neurons were an outlier among the populations tested.
claims.source: Hierarchical clustering supported this view: TS-projecting dopamine neurons were an outlier among the populations tested (Figure 5B).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by hierarchical clustering analysis shown in Figure 5B.

claims.claim: The inputs to TS-projecting dopamine neurons are dorso-laterally shifted compared to inputs to other populations of dopamine neurons.
claims.source: We found that, in several coronal planes along the A-P axis, the center of mass of labeled neurons differed between conditions. Interestingly, we observed that the inputs to TS-projecting dopamine neurons were shifted dorso-laterally compared to the inputs to other subpopulations (Figure 6).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by data shown in Figure 6.

claims.claim: In the anterior part of the brain, the dorso-lateral shift of inputs to TS-projecting dopamine neurons is caused by the relatively low number of inputs from the ventral striatum.
claims.source: In the anterior part of the brain, this shift is caused by the relatively low number of inputs from the ventral striatum to TS-projecting dopamine neurons (Figure 6A).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by data shown in Figure 6A.

claims.claim: In the middle sections of the brain, the dorso-lateral shift of inputs to TS-projecting dopamine neurons is caused by an increased number of inputs from GP and EP, as well as a decrease in inputs from the ventromedial hypothalamus.
claims.source: In the middle sections of the brain, the shift is caused by an increased number of inputs from GP (Figure 6B) and EP (Figure 6C), as well as a decrease in inputs from the ventromedial hypothalamus.
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by data shown in Figure 6B and 6C.

claims.claim: In a more posterior section of the brain, the dorso-lateral shift of inputs to TS-projecting dopamine neurons is caused by the large number of inputs from the subthalamic and parasubthalamic nuclei, as well as the lower number of inputs from the ventromedial hypothalamus.
claims.source: Finally, in a more posterior section of the brain, this shift is caused by the large number of inputs from the subthalamic and parasubthalamic nuclei to TS-projecting neurons (Figure 6D), as well as the lower number of inputs from the ventromedial hypothalamus.
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by data shown in Figure 6D.

claims.claim: The input pattern to TS-projecting dopamine neurons was unique, regardless of the method used for analysis.
claims.source: This suggests that the input pattern to TS-projecting dopamine neurons was unique, regardless of the method used for analysis.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from multiple analyses.

claims.claim: The inputs to subpopulations of dopamine neurons were topographically organized within and across nucleus boundaries.
claims.source: Although the meaning of the shift is not clear, overall, our analysis revealed that the inputs to subpopulations of dopamine neurons were topographically organized within and across nucleus boundaries.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the spatial analysis of inputs.

claims.claim: For each of the 'canonical' populations, between 12% and 20% of the input neurons were located in the ventral striatum whereas only 5% of the input neurons were located in the ventral striatum for TS-projecting dopamine neurons.
claims.source: For each of the 'canonical' populations, between 12% and 20% of the input neurons were located in the ventral striatum whereas only 5% of the input neurons were located in the ventral striatum for TS-projecting dopamine neurons (Figure 7D).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by data shown in Figure 7D.

claims.claim: The authors observed discrete peaks of high density within the nucleus accumbens that do not correspond to the boundaries of commonly delineated sub-areas of this region (i.e., 'core' or 'shell').
claims.source: Our labeling showed discrete peaks of high density within the nucleus accumbens that do not correspond to the boundaries of commonly delineated sub-areas of this region (i.e., 'core' or 'shell') (Figure 7E–H).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by data shown in Figure 7E-H.

claims.claim: Using precise 3D density plotting, the authors determined the exact number and locations of ventral patches: 5 total, with 3 in the anterior medial ventral shell, 1 in the medial core and 1 in the posterior lateral shell.
claims.source: In the present study, using precise 3D density plotting, we determined the exact number and locations of these patches: 5 total, with 3 in the anterior medial ventral shell, 1 in the medial core and 1 in the posterior lateral shell (Figure 7G,H, Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by data shown in Figure 7G, 7H, and Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: Dense patches of inputs were observed in all cases, with the exception of inputs to TS-projecting dopamine neurons.
claims.source: We observed these dense patches of inputs in all cases, with the exception of inputs to TS-projecting dopamine neurons (Figure 7A–C,J).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by data shown in Figure 7A-C and 7J.

claims.claim: Of the input neurons in the nucleus accumbens, 16–26% were localized to these patches for all of the 'canonical' populations.
claims.source: Of the input neurons in the nucleus accumbens, 16–26% were localized to these patches for all of the 'canonical' populations (Figure 7I).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by data shown in Figure 7I.

claims.claim: The few inputs that TS-projecting neurons did receive from the nucleus accumbens were not concentrated in patches.
claims.source: By contrast, the few inputs that TS-projecting neurons did receive from the nucleus accumbens were not concentrated in patches (Figure 7C,I,J).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by data shown in Figure 7C, 7I, and 7J.

claims.claim: Neurons in the ventral patches may play a key role in regulation of dopamine neurons, while TS-projecting dopamine neurons may be relatively disconnected from this regulatory system.
claims.source: Thus, whereas neurons in the ventral patches may play a key role in regulation of dopamine neurons, TS-projecting dopamine neurons may be relatively disconnected from this regulatory system.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the data on ventral patches.

claims.claim: Each subpopulation received inputs differentially from different patches.
claims.source: We next compared the distribution of inputs from these patches between different populations of dopamine neurons. We found that each subpopulation received inputs differentially from different patches.
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by data from the study.

claims.claim: mPFC-projecting dopamine neurons received a larger ratio of inputs from the most medial patch.
claims.source: For example, mPFC-projecting dopamine neurons received a larger ratio of inputs from the most medial patch, while Amy-projecting dopamine neurons received more of their inputs from the lateral patches (Figure 7J).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by data shown in Figure 7J.

claims.claim: Amy-projecting dopamine neurons received more of their inputs from the lateral patches.
claims.source: For example, mPFC-projecting dopamine neurons received a larger ratio of inputs from the most medial patch, while Amy-projecting dopamine neurons received more of their inputs from the lateral patches (Figure 7J).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by data shown in Figure 7J.

claims.claim: The authors did not observe that monosynaptic inputs accumulated in BFP-labeled areas (the projection sites).
claims.source: Surprisingly, we did not observe that monosynaptic inputs accumulated in BFP-labeled areas (Figure 8A–F).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by data shown in Figure 8A-F.

claims.claim: There was no statistically significant difference between the number of potential reciprocal inputs to each subpopulation and the average number of inputs in this area among all other subpopulations when comparing by nucleus.
claims.source: First, we compared how many inputs each population receives from the nucleus that it projects to. We found that there was some variability, but that no population received a statistically significantly higher fraction of inputs from the region that it projected to (Figure 8G).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by statistical analysis shown in Figure 8G.

claims.claim: There were no statistically significant differences when using the injection sites instead of the targeted nuclei to quantify reciprocal connections.
claims.source: Because some of our injections were limited to a portion of a region (for example, our injection into the DS only covered the anterior medial DS), we did a further analysis using the injection sites instead of the targeted nuclei to quantify the data. With this analysis, we also found no statistically significant differences (Figure 8H).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by statistical analysis shown in Figure 8H.

claims.claim: Reciprocal monosynaptic connections are not a defining characteristic of inputs to dopamine neurons with differing projection targets.
claims.source: In short, we observed that reciprocal monosynaptic connections are not a defining characteristic of inputs to dopamine neurons with differing projection targets (Figure 9).
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the reciprocity analysis, with reference to Figure 9.

claims.claim: Most dopamine neurons (besides TS-projecting dopamine neurons) have similar inputs regardless of their projection target.
claims.source: Rather, we found that most dopamine neurons (besides TS-projecting dopamine neurons) have similar inputs regardless of their projection target.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the overall data analysis.

claims.claim: Alheid and Heimer proposed that a major organizational principle of the brain is the existence of parallel functional and anatomical macrosystems.
claims.source: Alheid and Heimer proposed that a major organizational principle of the brain is the existence of parallel functional and anatomical macrosystems, each comprised of a cortical area, a cortical input nucleus (such as an area in the striatum), an output nucleus (such as a part of the pallidum), thalamus, and brainstem (Alheid and Heimer, 1988; Zahm, 2006).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior theoretical work.

claims.claim: In stark contrast to the proposal of parallel macrosystems, the authors found only loose reciprocity between dopamine neurons and their projection targets.
claims.source: In stark contrast to this proposal, we found only loose reciprocity between dopamine neurons and their projection targets.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the data analysis.

claims.claim: Reciprocal connectivity might not be the general mechanism of RPE computation and dopamine functions.
claims.source: In other words, reciprocal connectivity might not be the general mechanism of RPE computation and dopamine functions.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the lack of reciprocity observed.

claims.claim: Most dopamine neurons are more likely to gather information from a set of common sources and broadcast a common RPE to many brain areas.
claims.source: Our data suggests that neurons in cortex, striatum, pallidum, habenula, or amygdala may not 'entrain' different populations of dopamine neurons. Rather, most dopamine neurons are more likely to gather information from a set of common sources and broadcast a common RPE to many brain areas (Figure 9), while specific populations with different sets of inputs, such as TS-projecting dopamine neurons, might have different functions.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the data analysis, with reference to Figure 9.

claims.claim: Specific populations with different sets of inputs, such as TS-projecting dopamine neurons, might have different functions.
claims.source: Our data suggests that neurons in cortex, striatum, pallidum, habenula, or amygdala may not 'entrain' different populations of dopamine neurons. Rather, most dopamine neurons are more likely to gather information from a set of common sources and broadcast a common RPE to many brain areas (Figure 9), while specific populations with different sets of inputs, such as TS-projecting dopamine neurons, might have different functions.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the data analysis, with reference to Figure 9.

claims.claim: The ventral striatum was reported to receive a RPE signal from dopamine neurons.
claims.source: Because the ventral striatum was reported to receive a RPE signal from dopamine neurons (Roitman et al., 2008; Clark et al., 2012; Hart et al., 2014), we reasoned that finding the monosynaptic inputs to VS-projecting dopamine neurons would narrow down the list of inputs that are potentially important to RPE computation.
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior studies.

claims.claim: Many brain areas have the potential to directly modulate RPE in dopamine neurons.
claims.source: Based on this logic, many brain areas have the potential to directly modulate RPE in dopamine neurons.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the finding that many areas provide inputs to VS-projecting dopamine neurons.

claims.claim: The results suggest that dopamine neurons projecting to the anterior vs posterior part of the striatum receive distinct inputs.
claims.source: Our results suggest that dopamine neurons projecting to the anterior vs posterior part of the striatum receive distinct inputs.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the data analysis.

claims.claim: It has been shown that the anterior striatum is important for skill learning and the posterior part is important for skill execution in monkeys.
claims.source: For example, it has been shown that the anterior striatum is important for skill learning and the posterior part is important for skill execution in monkeys (Miyachi et al., 1997).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior work.

claims.claim: Kim and Hikosaka showed that the anterior caudate encodes flexible values, whereas the posterior caudate encodes stable values.

results.result: The authors developed and validated a projection-specific rabies tracing method combined with CLARITY and light-sheet microscopy to map monosynaptic inputs to eight subpopulations of dopamine neurons defined by their projection targets (VS, DS, TS, GP, Amy, OFC, mPFC, lHb).
results.evaluation: Claims C1, C19-C21, C25-C28, C30-C31, C34, and C169 collectively describe the methodological approach and validation. The method successfully restricted rabies infection to projection-specific dopamine neurons (98±1% TH-positive, C32) and enabled whole-brain mapping. The technical validation (C32-C34) and successful application to eight targets (C171) provide strong evidence for this methodological result.

results.result: Most dopamine neuron populations (excluding TS-projecting neurons) receive similar sets of inputs, with the basal ganglia (particularly ventral striatum) and hypothalamus (particularly lateral hypothalamus) providing the majority of inputs, and high correlations (r=0.85-0.98) between most population pairs.
results.evaluation: Claims C2, C22, C45-C48, C61, and C84 are supported by quantitative data showing similar input patterns across most populations. The correlation analysis (C61) and regional quantification (C45-C48) provide statistical support. However, the claim of 'similar' inputs requires careful interpretation given that some differences exist (C56-C60), though these are minor compared to the TS outlier.

results.result: TS-projecting dopamine neurons are a clear outlier, receiving significantly fewer inputs from ventral striatum and significantly more inputs from globus pallidus, subthalamic nucleus, and zona incerta, with consistently lower correlations (r=0.65-0.82) compared to other populations.
results.evaluation: Claims C4-C5, C23, C44, C49-C52, C54, C62-C63, and C68 are strongly supported by multiple statistical analyses including 1-way ANOVA with multiple comparison corrections (C51), t-tests (C54), correlation analysis (C62), and hierarchical clustering (C63). The convergence of evidence from different analytical approaches strengthens this conclusion.

results.result: TS-projecting dopamine neurons constitute a unique class of dopamine neurons regulated by different inputs, suggesting they may have different functions compared to other dopamine populations.
results.evaluation: Claims C6, C24, C55, C89, and C172 represent the main conclusion drawn from the anatomical data. This is well-supported by the convergent evidence from multiple analyses (input distribution, correlation, clustering, spatial analysis) showing TS-projecting neurons as consistent outliers. However, the functional implications remain speculative (C96-C98) and would require additional physiological studies.

results.result: Most dopamine neuron populations receive inputs from five discrete 'ventral patches' within the nucleus accumbens (16-26% of NAc inputs), with different populations receiving differential inputs from different patches, while TS-projecting neurons lack concentrated patch inputs.
results.evaluation: Claims C3, C70-C79 describe the ventral patch organization with specific quantitative data (C72: 5 patches with defined locations; C74: 16-26% of NAc inputs). The 3D density plotting methodology (C72) and consistent observation across populations (C73-C75) support this finding. The differential patch usage by different populations (C77-C79) adds functional significance.

results.result: Inputs to TS-projecting dopamine neurons are dorso-laterally shifted compared to other populations across multiple coronal planes, with this shift caused by reduced ventral striatum inputs anteriorly and increased GP/EP/STh inputs posteriorly.
results.evaluation: Claims C64-C67 and C69 describe spatial organization of inputs with specific anatomical explanations for the dorso-lateral shift at different anterior-posterior levels. The center-of-mass analysis provides quantitative support, though the biological significance of this topographic organization remains unclear (C69).

results.result: Reciprocal monosynaptic connections are not a defining characteristic of dopamine neuron circuitry; dopamine neurons do not preferentially receive inputs from their projection targets.
results.evaluation: Claims C80-C83, C86-C87 are supported by statistical analyses showing no significant enrichment of inputs from projection targets (C81-C82). This contradicts the parallel macrosystem model (C85-C86) and suggests alternative circuit organization. The analysis was performed both by nucleus and by injection site, strengthening the conclusion.

results.result: Most dopamine neurons likely gather information from common sources and broadcast common RPE signals to many brain areas, with ventral striatum inputs potentially providing 'expectation' signals that suppress dopamine responses when rewards are expected, while TS-projecting neurons may not be subject to this regulation.
results.evaluation: Claims C88, C91, C101-C102 represent functional interpretations of anatomical data. While the anatomical observations are well-supported, the functional implications regarding RPE computation and expectation signaling rely on prior models (C100) and remain speculative without physiological validation. The logic is sound but requires experimental testing.

results.result: Dopamine neurons with distinct projection targets reside in different but overlapping areas of the midbrain, with a dorso-lateral shift from VS to DS to TS projecting neurons, and most projection-specific populations distributed in both VTA and SNc.
results.evaluation: Claims C40-C43 and C136 describe the anatomical distribution of starter neurons. The overlapping distributions are consistent with prior literature (C40) and the control experiment (C43) confirms that transsynaptic spread did not cause nonspecific labeling. This validates the specificity of the projection-based classification.

results.result: TS-projecting dopamine neurons receive more inputs from STh, PSTh, and ZI, representing glutamatergic 'hyperdirect pathway' inputs, inhibitory 'indirect pathway' inputs from pallidum, and inputs from output nuclei (SNr/EP), suggesting cortical information is transmitted through different pathways than to other dopamine neurons.
results.evaluation: Claims C103, C106-C108, and C111 describe the unique input pathways to TS-projecting neurons with reference to established basal ganglia circuit organization (C104-C105). The anatomical data clearly show these differential inputs, and the interpretation in terms of direct/indirect/hyperdirect pathways is well-grounded in prior knowledge.

results.result: Among 'canonical' dopamine populations, subtle differences exist: DS-projecting neurons receive more neocortical inputs, VS-projecting neurons receive more inputs from olfactory tubercle and ventromedial hypothalamus, and lHb-projecting neurons receive fewer inputs from posterior midbrain regions.
results.evaluation: Claims C56-C60 describe minor differences among non-TS populations. While these differences are observable in the data (Figure 4), they did not reach statistical significance after multiple comparison correction (C53), suggesting they are real but subtle trends rather than defining features.

results.result: The tail of the striatum in mice may be homologous to the posterior putamen in primates, and the strong STh input to TS-projecting dopamine neurons could partially explain their specific vulnerability in Parkinson's disease.
results.evaluation: Claims C92, C120-C121, C124 represent speculative connections to Parkinson's disease. While the anatomical observations are solid (C120, C122), the homology claim (C121) and the mechanistic explanation for vulnerability (C124) are speculative and based on prior theories (C123) rather than direct evidence from this study.

results.result: TS-projecting dopamine neurons receive monosynaptic inputs preferentially from all main DBS target areas (STh, ZI, GPi/EP, PPTg), suggesting these sites might selectively influence TS-projecting circuits without affecting other dopamine functions.
results.evaluation: Claims C127-C130 connect the anatomical findings to DBS therapy. While the anatomical observation (C127) is supported by the data, the therapeutic implications (C128-C130) are highly speculative and would require clinical validation. The logic is reasonable but remains hypothetical.

results.result: The combination of CLARITY and light-sheet microscopy with automated cell detection and alignment allows for rapid, consistent, unbiased, and automated analysis of whole-brain tracing experiments.
results.evaluation: Claims C35-C39, C167-C168 describe the technical pipeline with specific success rates (C35: 87% clearing success). The methodology enabled systematic analysis of large datasets that would be impractical with traditional methods (C152-C153). The semi-automated approach represents a significant technical advance.

results.result: The projection-specific rabies tracing method achieved high specificity (98±1% TH-positive) and demonstrated that minute TVA expression from retrograde AAV infection is sufficient for subsequent rabies infection.
results.evaluation: Claims C32-C34 and C149 provide validation data for the method. The high TH-positivity (C32) and control experiments (C33) demonstrate specificity. However, this also reveals a limitation: the high efficiency means proper controls are essential (C150-C151) as even small TVA expression enables infection.

results.result: Recent related studies found similar input patterns among most dopamine subpopulations, consistent with the current findings, though neither examined TS-projecting neurons.
results.evaluation: Claims C131-C134 and C148 compare the current results with concurrent studies (Beier et al., 2015; Lerner et al., 2015). The consistency across independent studies using different methods strengthens confidence in the main finding that most dopamine populations have similar inputs, though methodological differences exist.

results.result: The viral tracing method may allow trans-synaptic spread between dopamine neurons, though intrinsic VTA/SNc connections originate mainly from non-dopamine neurons, and related studies using alternative methods found similar results.
results.evaluation: Claims C145-C147 acknowledge a potential limitation. While trans-synaptic spread between dopamine neurons could make populations appear more similar (C145), the fact that intrinsic connections are mainly from non-dopamine neurons (C146) and that studies with better controls found similar results (C147-C148) suggests this is not a major confound.

results.result: CLARITY was chosen over organic solvent-based clearing because it preserves GFP and tdTomato fluorescence and maintains brain morphology, though it causes loss of mCherry and BFP fluorescence and produces dimmer autofluorescence than iDISCO.
results.evaluation: Claims C162-C166 explain the rationale for method selection with specific observations about fluorophore preservation (C163). The trade-offs are clearly documented, showing that CLARITY was appropriate for the experimental goals despite some limitations.
